name: Persistent depressive disorder
summary: Depressed mood on most days for at least 2 years (1 year in youth) with at least two other depressive symptoms; DSM-5-TR merges dysthymia and chronic major depression into this diagnosis. No currently marketed US drug carries a PDD- or dysthymia-specific indication, so antidepressants approved for MDD are used off-label, usually with psychotherapy. Chronic depression responds less well and needs longer treatment trials than episodic MDD.
plainSummary: Persistent depressive disorder is long-lasting depression that goes on for two years or more. Talk therapy and antidepressant medicines, often used together, can help.
noApprovedNote: No FDA-approved medication currently on the US market has an indication specifically for persistent depressive disorder or dysthymia (checked on DailyMed and openFDA label indications, 2026-10-11). The only US label found that named 'dysthymic disorder' was maprotiline (Ludiomil and generics: 'depressive neurosis (dysthymic disorder)'), and Drugs@FDA lists every maprotiline application as discontinued. Some older tricyclic labels (e.g., doxepin: 'psychoneurotic patients with depression') use outdated terms that overlap historically but do not name PDD. When a PDD patient also meets criteria for a current major depressive episode, MDD-approved antidepressants are on-label for that episode.

offLabel.use: First-line pharmacotherapy for chronic depressive symptoms/dysthymia, alone or combined with CBT
offLabel.notes: NICE NG222 (1.10.2) lists SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, CBT, or CBT plus an SSRI or TCA as options for chronic depressive symptoms that impair functioning. If one SSRI is not tolerated, NICE suggests trying another SSRI. A network meta-analysis (Kriston 2014) found SSRIs better than placebo for PDD. Responses are slower and smaller than in episodic MDD. Antidepressant boxed warning applies to youth and young adults.

details.labeledFor: SSRIs are FDA-approved for major depressive disorder; none is specifically labeled for persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).

dosing.start: Sertraline 25–50 mg, fluoxetine 10–20 mg, escitalopram 5–10 mg, or paroxetine 10 mg
dosing.target: Usual MDD ranges (sertraline 50–200, fluoxetine 20–60, escitalopram 10–20, paroxetine 20–50 mg)

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: MAOI use within 14 days (or linezolid / IV methylene blue)
warnings: Early activation or anxiety, GI upset, sexual dysfunction
Hyponatremia and bleeding risk (higher with NSAIDs/anticoagulants)
Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs
details.plainSummary: SSRIs are the usual first medicines for long-lasting low mood. Improvement is often slower and smaller than in short depressive episodes.

references.label: NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022), section 1.10 Chronic depressive symptoms
Kriston et al. Acute treatments for persistent depressive disorder: network meta-analysis. Depress Anxiety 2014, PubMed

offLabel.notes: NICE NG222 lists SNRIs among first options for chronic depressive symptoms. PDD-specific RCT data are thinner than for SSRIs or TCAs. Watch blood pressure (venlafaxine) and discontinuation symptoms. Antidepressant boxed warning applies.

details.labeledFor: Venlafaxine and duloxetine are FDA-approved for major depressive disorder (and anxiety); not specifically for persistent depressive disorder.

dosing.notes: Check blood pressure (venlafaxine); taper to stop.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: MAOI use within 14 days (or linezolid / IV methylene blue)
details.plainSummary: SNRI antidepressants are another option for long-lasting depression; blood pressure should be checked.

references.label: NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022), section 1.10

offLabel.use: Chronic depression/dysthymia, including after SSRI non-response
offLabel.notes: NICE NG222 lists TCAs as an option but warns that they are dangerous in overdose. In a large RCT in chronic depression, sertraline and imipramine were similarly effective, with sertraline better tolerated. Cautions: anticholinergic effects, orthostasis, cardiac conduction effects; check ECG in at-risk patients; limit amounts dispensed when suicide risk is present.

details.labeledFor: Imipramine is FDA-approved for depression and childhood enuresis; not specifically for persistent depressive disorder.

dosing.target: 100–200 mg/day (trials used up to about 200 mg)
dosing.notes: ECG in at-risk patients; limit dispensed quantity when suicide risk is present.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: Acute recovery period after myocardial infarction
warnings: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion)
Orthostasis and cardiac conduction effects; ECG in at-risk patients
Lowers the seizure threshold; may trigger mania
Highly toxic in overdose; limit quantities
details.plainSummary: An older antidepressant that works about as well as an SSRI for long-lasting depression but has more side effects and is dangerous in overdose.

references.label: NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022), section 1.10
Keller et al. Treatment of chronic depression, part 2: sertraline vs imipramine RCT. J Clin Psychiatry 1998, PubMed

offLabel.use: Chronic depressive symptoms not responding to SSRIs/SNRIs, in specialist settings
offLabel.notes: NICE NG222 (1.10.6) lists irreversible MAOIs as alternatives in specialist settings after non-response to SSRIs/SNRIs. Requires dietary tyramine restriction, careful interaction management, and adequate washout periods when switching (serotonin syndrome, hypertensive crisis risk).

details.labeledFor: Phenelzine is FDA-approved for atypical or treatment-resistant depression; not specifically for persistent depressive disorder.

dosing.start: 15 mg once to three times daily
dosing.notes: Tyramine-restricted diet; at least 14 days washout from other antidepressants (5 weeks from fluoxetine).

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: Pheochromocytoma, heart failure, liver disease or abnormal liver tests
Sympathomimetics, SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, bupropion, buspirone, dextromethorphan, meperidine
warnings: Hypertensive crisis with tyramine or sympathomimetics
details.plainSummary: A strong older antidepressant reserved for specialist care. It requires a strict diet and careful checking of other medicines to avoid dangerous reactions.

references.label: NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022), section 1.10

offLabel.agent: Low-dose amisulpride (not available in the US)
offLabel.notes: NICE NG222 lists low-dose amisulpride (max 50 mg/day) as an alternative in specialist settings, and network meta-analysis supports efficacy in PDD. Oral amisulpride for psychiatric use is not marketed in the US (only an IV antiemetic product exists). Risks include hyperprolactinemia and QT prolongation, and higher doses may worsen depression.

details.labeledFor: Oral amisulpride is not marketed in the US (an IV formulation is approved for postoperative nausea/vomiting); available elsewhere for schizophrenia.

dosing.max: 50 mg/day (higher doses are antipsychotic-range and may worsen depression)
dosing.notes: Not available as an oral psychiatric drug in the US.

formulations: Outside the US: tablets 50, 100, 200, 400 mg; oral solution
contraindications: Not applicable in the US; outside the US: phaeochromocytoma, prolactin-dependent tumors, QT-prolonging drugs
warnings: Class warning: increased mortality in older adults with dementia
details.plainSummary: A low-dose antipsychotic used for long-lasting low mood in some countries. It is not available as a pill for this use in the US.

references.label: NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022), section 1.10
Kriston et al. Network meta-analysis of acute PDD treatments. Depress Anxiety 2014, PubMed
